title: The Arrival in Madinah
subtitle: The Oasis of Quba, the Triumphant Entry, and the Hospitality of Abu Ayyub
summary: The longing wait of the Ansar on the volcanic plains, the joy of sighting the Prophet at Quba, founding the first mosque of Islam, the triumphant Friday entry into Madinah, the camel Qaswa choosing her resting place, and the humble hospitality of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari.

sections.text: The Longing on the Volcanic Plain

For days after news leaked from Makkah that the Prophet had departed, the believers in Yathrib lived in eager anticipation. Every morning following the dawn prayer, crowds of the Ansar and early Muhajirun walked out to the volcanic lava plains of Al-Harrah on the southern approaches of the city. Under the scorching desert sun, they shaded their eyes and scanned the southern horizon until the sweltering midday heat forced them back into their homes.

The sirah commonly gives the day as Monday, the twelfth of Rabi al-Awwal. Reports differ on the weekday and the date, and a single day of that month is not the same thing as a named day in September 622. After the people had gone back indoors, a Jewish man on a fortress roof saw the two travelers and called out to Banu Qaylah — the Aws and the Khazraj — 'Here is your fortune, the honor you have been waiting for.' The Arabic word is jadd, fortune and standing, not a grandfather. The people came out to meet the Prophet.
The tranquil date groves of Quba where the Prophet rested after the grueling migration.
The Oasis of Quba and the First Mosque

The Prophet halted first at the outlying southern village of Quba, staying as a guest at the home of Kulthum ibn al-Hadm of the Banu Amr ibn Awf clan. As crowds converged, many who had never seen the Prophet mistook the gray-haired Abu Bakr for him; but when the sun rose higher and Abu Bakr stepped forward to shade the Prophet with his cloak, the people instantly recognized the Messenger of God.

During the stay at Quba, which the sirah gives as about four days, he laid the foundations of Masjid Quba, the first mosque of the Hijrah. Surah al-Tawbah 9:108 speaks of a mosque founded on mindfulness of God from the first day. Readers have long discussed whether that mosque is Quba or the Prophet's mosque in Madinah. A report in Sahih Muslim has the Prophet point to his own mosque when he was asked, while the people of Quba are praised for their care in purification. The verse also answers the affair of Masjid Dirar. The identification is not treated here as unanimous. The wording of the verse is:

لَّمَسْجِدٌ أُسِّسَ عَلَى التَّقْوَىٰ مِنْ أَوَّلِ يَوْمٍ أَحَقُّ أَن تَقُومَ فِيهِ ۚ فِيهِ رِجَالٌ يُحِبُّونَ أَن يَتَطَهَّرُوا ۚ وَاللَّهُ يُحِبُّ الْمُطَّهِّرِينَ
'A mosque founded on righteousness from the first day is more worthy for you to stand in. Within it are men who love to purify themselves; and God loves those who purify themselves.' (Surah At-Tawbah 9:108)

It was also during this stay that Ali ibn Abi Talib reunited with the Prophet, having walked the entire three hundred miles from Makkah on foot by night, his feet raw and swollen, after dutifully returning every trust to its owner in Makkah.
The Triumphant Procession into the City

On Friday morning, mounted upon his she-camel Al-Qaswa, the Prophet set out toward the central heart of Yathrib. On the way, as the hour of midday prayer arrived in the valley of Ranuna among Banu Salim ibn Awf, the Prophet gathered approximately one hundred believers and delivered his first Friday sermon (Khutbah) in Madinah, leading them in the inaugural Jum'ah prayer.

As the procession entered the city proper, scenes of indescribable jubilation unfolded. Anas ibn Malik recounted: 'I witnessed the day the Messenger of God entered Madinah; never had I seen a day more luminous or beautiful!' Men, women, and children climbed atop rooftops and lined the thoroughfares, singing poetic verses of welcoming praise:

طَلَعَ الْبَدْرُ عَلَيْنَا * مِنْ ثَنِيَّاتِ الْوَدَاعِ
وَجَبَ الشُّكْرُ عَلَيْنَا * مَا دَعَا لِلَّهِ دَاعِ
'The full moon has risen over us from the passes of al-Wada. Gratitude is due from us so long as a caller calls upon God.' These lines are a well-known welcome. Their use on the day he entered from Quba is disputed: Thaniyyat al-Wada is the northern approach, and the arrival from Quba was from the south. They are kept as a popular traditional report, not as a settled record of that morning.
The lively streets and palm courtyards of Madinah where the inhabitants welcomed the Prophet.
The Camel's Choice and Abu Ayyub's Honor

As the Prophet rode through the city, the chieftains of every prominent clan stepped forward in turn, taking hold of Al-Qaswa's reins and pleading: 'Stay with us, O Messenger of God! We possess numbers, weapons, and strong protection!' To each chieftain, the Prophet smiled graciously and replied: 'Let her go, for she is divinely commanded (Da'uha fa innaha ma'murah).'

The camel walked forward with loose reins through the quarters of Madinah until she reached an open drying-yard belonging to two orphan boys, Sahl and Suhayl, of the Banu Najjar clan—the maternal relatives of the Prophet's grandfather Abd al-Muttalib. The beast knelt, arose, turned in a small circle, and knelt down once more, resting her neck upon the ground. The Prophet said: 'Here, if God wills, shall be the dwelling.'

Seeing the camel kneel before his door, Abu Ayyub Khalid ibn Zayd al-Ansari rushed forward joyfully, lifted the Prophet's travel luggage, and carried it into his two-story home. When other companions contended for the honor of hosting the guest, the Prophet smiled warmly and remarked: 'A man stays with his baggage.'

The Prophet lodged on the ground floor of Abu Ayyub's home for seven months until his mosque and modest living quarters were constructed. Abu Ayyub and his wife showed extraordinary reverence, trembling even to walk heavily upon the upper floor lest dust fall upon the Messenger of God below. From this arrival the oasis came to be called al-Madinah, the city of the Prophet.

references.title: The Holy Quran
